subject: health
title: Launch and diagnostic: dimensions of health
essentialQuestion: How can the dimensions of health help us understand a situation and choose a safe next step?
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible response tool
the lesson cards included on this page
learningGoal: I can name five dimensions of health, explain how they can affect one another, and use facts to choose a safe next step in a fictional situation.
keyPoints: Health has connected dimensions. Physical, mental, emotional, social, and environmental health are five useful ways to notice what may affect wellbeing.
A dimension is a category for thinking. It is not a score or a label for a person.
Use facts from the situation. Do not guess a person's health, feelings, motives, or character from one detail.
A safe next step may include asking a parent, guardian, teacher, school staff member, or another trusted adult for help. A health professional gives medical advice.
privacySafeScenario: All required work uses short fictional situations. The learner never has to describe personal health, body information, feelings, treatment, or family life.
studentTask: Read a fresh fictional situation. Name the dimensions that connect to the facts. Choose a safe next step. Explain the choice with two facts and name an adult who could help if help is needed.
knowledgeCheck: Explain why one fact cannot show a person's whole health. Then apply the five-dimension idea to a new fictional situation.
completionCriteria: I name at least two dimensions that fit the facts in the fresh situation.
I use two facts from the situation and do not turn a guess into a fact.
I choose a safe, respectful next step and explain why it fits.
I name a trusted adult or qualified professional when the situation needs help.

lessonExperience.learnerTitle: How the dimensions of health work together
lessonExperience.privacyNotice: You will only write about fictional people. Keep private health and family information private.

entryCheck.heading: Start with what you notice
entryCheck.directions: Choose the sentence that uses a fact instead of a guess.
choices: The community room is noisy today.
Jordan does not care about the group.
entryCheck.support: A fact is something the situation tells you or something you can observe. A guess adds an idea that the situation did not give you.
entryCheck.treatment: This warm-up is not scored. Use the support before you continue if you need it.

explanation.heading: Health is a connected picture
paragraphs: Health means wellbeing. Wellbeing is how a person is doing in different parts of life. No single moment tells us a person's whole health.
We can use five dimensions to study a situation: physical, mental, emotional, social, and environmental. The dimensions can affect one another.
A dimension is a thinking category. It is not a grade, a body score, or a label for a person. People also have different needs, supports, and surroundings.
Use facts before you choose an action. If a situation may be unsafe or needs expert help, pause and ask a trusted adult. A qualified health professional gives medical advice.
explanation.importantDistinction: A situation can affect a dimension of health without proving anything about a person's complete health or a medical condition.
explanation.decisionRule: FACTS: Name what the situation tells you. CONNECT: Link the facts to one or more dimensions. CHOOSE: Pick a safe and respectful action. ASK: Name an adult or professional who can help when needed.

terms.meaning: how the body works and is cared for
terms.boundary: It is not a judgment about body size or appearance.

terms.meaning: wellbeing connected to thinking, learning, and handling challenges
terms.example: using a quiet place to focus on a task
terms.boundary: One hard moment does not tell us that a person has a condition.

terms.meaning: noticing, naming, and expressing feelings in safe ways
terms.example: telling a trusted adult that a situation feels upsetting
terms.boundary: Feelings are not right or wrong.

terms.meaning: wellbeing connected to relationships, communication, and support
terms.example: listening and asking a group member what help is useful
terms.boundary: One disagreement does not define a person or a relationship.

terms.meaning: how surroundings can affect safety and wellbeing
terms.example: moving away from heavy smoke with an adult's help
terms.boundary: It describes surroundings, not a person's worth.

vocabularyCheck.heading: Check the words
vocabularyCheck.directions: Match each fact to the dimension it most clearly shows. More than one dimension may connect, but choose the closest one for this quick check.

items.prompt: A library opens a quiet room for students to work.
A friend listens and helps another person find a trusted adult.
A park closes a path because storm damage made it unsafe.

vocabularyCheck.selfCheck: Say the meaning of the dimension in your own words. Then point to the fact that matches that meaning.

modelExample.heading: Watch the thinking: Kai's library plan
modelExample.situation: Kai's class plans to finish a group poster in the library. Construction makes the library very noisy. The teacher says the group may use a quieter classroom. Kai cannot hear the group's ideas in the library.
possibleActions: Assume Kai has a health condition.
Ask the teacher to move the group to the quieter classroom.
Tell Kai to work alone without asking what would help.

thinkingSteps.label: 1. Name the facts
thinkingSteps.text: The library is noisy. Kai cannot hear the group. The teacher offered a quieter room. I do not add a guess about Kai.

thinkingSteps.label: 2. Connect the dimensions
thinkingSteps.text: The noise is an environmental fact. Hearing and sharing ideas connect to mental and social health.

thinkingSteps.label: 3. Compare safe options
thinkingSteps.text: Moving uses an option the teacher already approved. It helps the whole group hear without labeling Kai or leaving Kai out.

thinkingSteps.label: 4. Choose and ask
thinkingSteps.text: I would ask the teacher to move the group. The teacher is the right adult because the teacher controls the class spaces.

modelExample.successCheck: The response uses facts, names connected dimensions, gives a reason, and uses the right adult support. It does not guess about Kai's health.

guidedReasoning.heading: Try it with support
guidedReasoning.situation: Maya's science club is meeting outside. A strong wind starts blowing loose papers and small branches. The club leader says everyone may move into the community room.
turnOne: Name two facts from the situation.
Choose the dimension that most clearly connects to the changing surroundings.
guidedReasoning.cue: Look for what changed, what choices are available, and which adult has responsibility for the meeting.
feedbackMoves: If you wrote a guess, replace it with words the situation gives you.
If you named a dimension, explain how one fact connects to its meaning.
If your action is safe, add the adult or help source that makes it possible.
guidedReasoning.turnTwo: Revise one sentence so it includes a fact, a dimension, and a safe action.
guidedReasoning.releaseCondition: Continue when your revised sentence uses a stated fact and does not label Maya.

independentEvidence.heading: Show what you know
independentEvidence.situation: Leah's group is making a poster at a community center. A large event starts in the same room. The group cannot hear one another. A center leader offers them an open table in a quieter room.
directions: Write two facts from the situation.
Name at least two dimensions that connect to those facts.
Choose a safe and respectful next step.
Explain your choice with the facts.
Name an adult who can help if help is needed.
permittedSupports: typing, handwriting, drawing with labels, signing, or telling an adult who is helping with the lesson
a break, extra time, or a low-distraction space
independentEvidence.independenceBoundary: For this check, another person may restate the directions but may not choose the dimensions, action, facts, or reason for you.
successCriteria: I use at least two facts.
I connect at least two dimensions to the facts.
I choose a safe, respectful action and give a reason.
I name the right kind of adult support when help is needed.

freshConceptCheck.heading: Check what you know
freshConceptCheck.situation: Omar's class reaches a park for a cleanup. A sign says one path is closed because a storm damaged it. The teacher points to a different open path.
directions: Explain why the closed path is an environmental health fact, not a judgment about Omar.
Choose a safe next step and support it with one fact.
Name who has authority to guide the class.
freshConceptCheck.freshnessNote: This is a new situation. Do not copy the library model.

remediation.heading: Try a different way
remediation.trigger: Use this section if you mixed up a dimension and a judgment, used a guess as a fact, or left out a safe support route.
remediation.alternateExplanation: Picture five clear windows looking at one fictional situation. Each window helps you notice a different kind of fact. A window shows part of the picture. It does not score or label the person. First use the camera test: Could a camera or the written situation show this fact? Then use the window test: Which dimension helps explain why the fact matters?
contrast: Fact: The hallway lights are off. Guess: Everyone in the hallway is careless.
Dimension: The dark hallway is an environmental health concern. Label: A person in the hallway is unhealthy.
remediation.guidedCorrection: Change this guess into a fact: 'The students do not care about safety.' Use only this information: A spill sign is beside a wet floor.

freshRetry.situation: A youth center's water fountain is closed for repair. A staff member points to a working fountain in the next room.
directions: Connect the fact to one dimension.
Choose a safe next step and name the adult support.

remediation.exitCriterion: Return to the lesson check when you can write a fact, connect a dimension, and choose a safe action without labeling a person.

laterTransfer.timing: Use in a later lesson or another session.
laterTransfer.prompt: In a new fictional case, identify two connected dimensions, separate facts from guesses, and explain a safe action plus the right support route.
laterTransfer.masteryBoundary: This lesson's independent response is one evidence occasion. Mastery needs accurate independent evidence on this lesson and on the later transfer.

adaptationChoices: Keep the health idea the same while changing how the learner reads or responds. Offer read-aloud, shorter chunks, vocabulary cards, text-to-speech, speech-to-text, typing, handwriting, drawing with labels, signing, or telling an adult who is helping with the lesson. A support may restate a direction but may not supply the dimension, fact, safe choice, or reason during independent work.
extensionChallenge: Write a new fictional case in which one environmental fact connects to two other dimensions. Include enough facts, choices, and adult support for another learner to reason safely. Do not use a real person's private information.
accessibilitySupports: Read each short section aloud or use text-to-speech.
Show one direction at a time and allow extra time or a break.
Use a five-part labeled diagram for the dimensions.
Accept typing, handwriting, drawing with labels, signing, or telling an adult who is helping with the lesson for equal credit.
Do not lower credit because the learner uses an adaptation, translator, communication support, or trusted adult.
trustedAdultNote: If a real situation feels unsafe or raises a health concern, pause the lesson and tell a parent, guardian, teacher, school staff member, or another trusted adult. A qualified health professional gives medical advice. In an emergency, get an adult and use the local emergency service.

optionalReflection.prompt: Optional and private: Draw five empty circles for the dimensions. Add one made-up example to any circle. Keep the page for yourself. You do not need to tell anyone that you did this.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, body comparison, or appearance scoring.
This task never requires calorie counting, dieting, or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires sharing medical history, a diagnosis, treatment, medication, feelings, family conflict, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
This task never requires advice about an individual learner's treatment, medication, food, supplement, or exercise plan.

contentProvenance.objective: Teach the five connected dimensions of health before collecting fresh, privacy-safe concept and decision evidence.
